When used as a verb, to kneecap someone or something means to deliberately cripple, weaken, or sabotage it — to damage it in a targeted way that stops it from functioning properly, especially while leaving it technically still alive or existing.

Think of it this way: you're not destroying something completely. You're hitting it in a critical spot so that it can no longer stand on its own.

Your kneecap is one of the most important joints in your body. Damage it, and you can't walk. You're not dead — but you're severely, perhaps permanently, limited.

This gave rise to the literal use of the verb first: to kneecap someone physically meant to shoot or strike them in the knee — a brutal act used as a punishment or torture method, especially by paramilitary groups, designed to cause lasting disability without killing the person. The victim survives, but is crippled.

That visceral image then crossed over into figurative language, which is where the word does most of its work today.
The Figurative Meaning (The Main One You'll Encounter)

To kneecap something means to deliberately undermine, sabotage, or severely weaken it — usually through a specific targeted action — so that it cannot operate at full strength or reach its potential.

The key qualities baked into this word are:

  • It is deliberate. This is never an accident. Someone chose to do this.
  • It is targeted. It strikes at something specific and critical.
  • It cripples without necessarily destroying. The thing still exists, but is now hobbled.
  • It is often seen as unfair or underhanded. The word carries a strong negative charge.

"The last-minute budget cuts effectively kneecapped the project before it even launched."

— The project still exists, but the cuts removed what it needed to succeed.

"Critics accused the government of kneecapping the investigation by refusing to release key documents."

— The investigation continues, but it's been crippled.

"The trade restrictions kneecapped the company's ability to compete internationally."

— The company still operates, but a vital capability has been taken out.

"He felt kneecapped by his own team, who kept blocking his proposals."

— He's still working, but rendered ineffective by internal sabotage.

This is a vivid, punchy, informal-to-mid-register word. It's used in journalism, political commentary, business writing, and casual conversation — but you'd be unlikely to find it in a legal contract or academic paper. It carries a sharp, even aggressive edge, which is exactly why writers reach for it: it communicates betrayal, sabotage, and unfairness all at once, more powerfully than words like "weaken" or "undermine."
What Makes It Different From Similar Words

WordWhat it implies
UndermineGradual erosion of strength or confidence
SabotageDeliberate destruction, often covert
HamstringRestrict freedom of action (very similar to kneecap)
KneecapTargeted, crippling blow — deliberate, unfair, leaves victim alive but weakened

(The closest synonym is hamstring, which also uses a body-part metaphor for crippling something. "Kneecap" tends to feel slightly more violent and sudden in tone.)

To kneecap something = to deliberately strike it in a critical way that cripples its ability to function, without necessarily destroying it entirely — always intentional, always unfair, always damaging.
